stem:
Calculate the equilibrium constant of the reaction:
\(\text{Cu}(s) + 2\text{Ag}^{+}(aq) \rightarrow \text{Cu}^{2+}(aq) + 2\text{Ag}(s)\)
\(E^{\circ}_{(cell)} = 0.46\,\text{V}\)

The standard electrode potential for Daniell cell is \(1.1\,\text{V}\). Calculate the standard Gibbs energy for the reaction:
\(\text{Zn}(s) + \text{Cu}^{2+}(aq) \rightarrow \text{Zn}^{2+}(aq) + \text{Cu}(s)\)
solution:
\(\Delta_r G^{\circ} = -nFE^{\circ}_{(cell)}\)

\(n\) in the above equation is 2, \(F = 96487\,\text{C mol}^{-1}\) and \(E^{\circ}_{(cell)} = 1.1\,\text{V}\)

Therefore, \(\Delta_r G^{\circ} = -2 \times 1.1\,\text{V} \times 96487\,\text{C mol}^{-1}\)

\(= -21227\,\text{J mol}^{-1}\)

\(= -212.27\,\text{kJ mol}^{-1}\)
_note: PRINTED DEFECT, transcribed faithfully: the intermediate line reads \(-21227\,\text{J mol}^{-1}\), which has lost a digit. \(2 \times 1.1 \times 96487 = 212271.4\), so the line should read \(-212271\,\text{J mol}^{-1}\). The book's own FINAL answer \(-212.27\,\text{kJ mol}^{-1}\) is correct and follows from the corrected intermediate, not from the printed one (which would give \(-21.227\,\text{kJ mol}^{-1}\)), so the defect is confined to that one line.

stem: Calculate the potential of hydrogen electrode in contact with a solution whose pH is 10.

\(\text{Ni}(s) + 2\text{Ag}^{+}(0.002\,\text{M}) \rightarrow \text{Ni}^{2+}(0.160\,\text{M}) + 2\text{Ag}(s)\)
Given that \(E^{\circ}_{cell} = 1.05\,\text{V}\)

The cell in which the following reaction occurs:
\(2\text{Fe}^{3+}(aq) + 2\text{I}^{-}(aq) \rightarrow 2\text{Fe}^{2+}(aq) + \text{I}_2(s)\)
has \(E^{\circ}_{cell} = 0.236\,\text{V}\) at \(298\,\text{K}\). Calculate the standard Gibbs energy and the equilibrium constant of the cell reaction.

Resistance of a conductivity cell filled with \(0.1\,\text{mol L}^{-1}\) \(\text{KCl}\) solution is \(100\,\Omega\). If the resistance of the same cell when filled with \(0.02\,\text{mol L}^{-1}\) \(\text{KCl}\) solution is \(520\,\Omega\), calculate the conductivity and molar conductivity of \(0.02\,\text{mol L}^{-1}\) \(\text{KCl}\) solution. The conductivity of \(0.1\,\text{mol L}^{-1}\) \(\text{KCl}\) solution is \(1.29\,\text{S/m}\).
solution:
The cell constant is given by the equation:

Cell constant \(= G^{*} =\) conductivity \(\times\) resistance

\(= 1.29\,\text{S/m} \times 100\,\Omega = 129\,\text{m}^{-1} = 1.29\,\text{cm}^{-1}\)

Conductivity of \(0.02\,\text{mol L}^{-1}\) \(\text{KCl}\) solution \(=\) cell constant \(/\) resistance

\(= \dfrac{G^{*}}{R} = \dfrac{129\,\text{m}^{-1}}{520\,\Omega} = 0.248\,\text{S m}^{-1}\)

Concentration \(= 0.02\,\text{mol L}^{-1} = 1000 \times 0.02\,\text{mol m}^{-3} = 20\,\text{mol m}^{-3}\)

Molar conductivity \(= \Lambda_m = \dfrac{\kappa}{c} = \dfrac{248 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{S m}^{-1}}{20\,\text{mol m}^{-3}} = 124 \times 10^{-4}\,\text{S m}^{2}\,\text{mol}^{-1}\)

Alternatively, \(\kappa = \dfrac{1.29\,\text{cm}^{-1}}{520\,\Omega} = 0.248 \times 10^{-2}\,\text{S cm}^{-1}\)

and \(\Lambda_m = \kappa \times 1000\,\text{cm}^{3}\,\text{L}^{-1}\,\text{molarity}^{-1}\)

\(= \dfrac{0.248 \times 10^{-2}\,\text{S cm}^{-1} \times 1000\,\text{cm}^{3}\,\text{L}^{-1}}{0.02\,\text{mol L}^{-1}} = 124\,\text{S cm}^{2}\,\text{mol}^{-1}\)

stem: The electrical resistance of a column of \(0.05\,\text{mol L}^{-1}\) \(\text{NaOH}\) solution of diameter \(1\,\text{cm}\) and length \(50\,\text{cm}\) is \(5.55 \times 10^{3}\,\text{ohm}\). Calculate its resistivity, conductivity and molar conductivity.
solution:
\(A = \pi r^{2} = 3.14 \times 0.5^{2}\,\text{cm}^{2} = 0.785\,\text{cm}^{2} = 0.785 \times 10^{-4}\,\text{m}^{2}\)

\(l = 50\,\text{cm} = 0.5\,\text{m}\)

\(R = \dfrac{\rho l}{A}\) or \(\rho = \dfrac{RA}{l} = \dfrac{5.55 \times 10^{3}\,\Omega \times 0.785\,\text{cm}^{2}}{50\,\text{cm}} = 87.135\,\Omega\,\text{cm}\)

Conductivity \(= \kappa = \dfrac{1}{\rho} = \left(\dfrac{1}{87.135}\right)\,\text{S cm}^{-1} = 0.01148\,\text{S cm}^{-1}\)

Molar conductivity, \(\Lambda_m = \dfrac{\kappa \times 1000}{c}\,\text{cm}^{3}\,\text{L}^{-1}\)

\(= \dfrac{0.01148\,\text{S cm}^{-1} \times 1000\,\text{cm}^{3}\,\text{L}^{-1}}{0.05\,\text{mol L}^{-1}} = 229.6\,\text{S cm}^{2}\,\text{mol}^{-1}\)

If we want to calculate the values of different quantities in terms of 'm' instead of 'cm',

\(\rho = \dfrac{RA}{l} = \dfrac{5.55 \times 10^{3}\,\Omega \times 0.785 \times 10^{-4}\,\text{m}^{2}}{0.5\,\text{m}} = 87.135 \times 10^{-2}\,\Omega\,\text{m}\)

\(\kappa = \dfrac{1}{\rho} = \dfrac{100}{87.135}\,\Omega\,\text{m} = 1.148\,\text{S m}^{-1}\)

and \(\Lambda_m = \dfrac{\kappa}{c} = \dfrac{1.148\,\text{S m}^{-1}}{50\,\text{mol m}^{-3}} = 229.6 \times 10^{-4}\,\text{S m}^{2}\,\text{mol}^{-1}\).
_note: Printed looseness carried faithfully: in the SI half of the solution the book writes the reciprocal of the resistivity as \(\kappa = 100/87.135\,\Omega\,\text{m}\), i.e. it keeps the resistivity's unit \(\Omega\,\text{m}\) where the reciprocal unit \(\text{S m}^{-1}\) belongs. The stated result \(1.148\,\text{S m}^{-1}\) is correct and carries the right unit; only the intermediate line's unit is wrong as printed.

stem:
The molar conductivity of \(\text{KCl}\) solutions at different concentrations at \(298\,\text{K}\) are given below:

| \(c/\text{mol L}^{-1}\) | \(\Lambda_m/\text{S cm}^{2}\,\text{mol}^{-1}\) |
|---|---|
| 0.000198 | 148.61 |
| 0.000309 | 148.29 |
| 0.000521 | 147.81 |
| 0.000989 | 147.09 |

Show that a plot between \(\Lambda_m\) and \(c^{1/2}\) is a straight line. Determine the values of \(\Lambda_m^{\circ}\) and \(A\) for \(\text{KCl}\).
solution:
Taking the square root of concentration we obtain:

| \(c^{1/2}/(\text{mol L}^{-1})^{1/2}\) | \(\Lambda_m/\text{S cm}^{2}\,\text{mol}^{-1}\) |
|---|---|
| 0.01407 | 148.61 |
| 0.01758 | 148.29 |
| 0.02283 | 147.81 |
| 0.03145 | 147.09 |

A plot of \(\Lambda_m\) (\(y\)-axis) and \(c^{1/2}\) (\(x\)-axis) is shown in (Fig. 3.7).

It can be seen that it is nearly a straight line. From the intercept (\(c^{1/2} = 0\)), we find that

\(\Lambda_m^{\circ} = 150.0\,\text{S cm}^{2}\,\text{mol}^{-1}\) and

\(A = -\,\text{slope} = 87.46\,\text{S cm}^{2}\,\text{mol}^{-1}/(\text{mol/L}^{-1})^{1/2}\).
_note: Two printed oddities, both carried faithfully. (1) STALE CROSS-REFERENCE: the solution says the plot 'is shown in (Fig. 3.7)', but the figure printed inside this very example box on the same page (p-17) is captioned 'Fig. 2.7: Variation of \(\Lambda_m\) against \(c^{1/2}\)'. 'Fig. 3.7' is a leftover from an edition in which Electrochemistry was chapter 3 — the same stale numbering that appears in Eg 2.7's 'Table 3.4'. (2) The unit printed for \(A\) is \((\text{mol/L}^{-1})^{1/2}\), which mixes the two forms; it should read \((\text{mol/L})^{1/2}\) or equivalently \((\text{mol L}^{-1})^{1/2}\), as the book itself writes in the solution's own table heading one paragraph above and on the graph's x-axis label. No _figure attached: the stem carries its own data table and the solution states both required values, so the row is answerable without the graph.

stem: Calculate \(\Lambda_m^{\circ}\) for \(\text{CaCl}_2\) and \(\text{MgSO}_4\) from the data given in Table 3.4.
solution:
We know from Kohlrausch law that

\(\Lambda_{m(\text{CaCl}_2)}^{\circ} = \lambda_{\text{Ca}^{2+}}^{\circ} + 2\lambda_{\text{Cl}^{-}}^{\circ} = 119.0\,\text{S cm}^{2}\,\text{mol}^{-1} + 2(76.3)\,\text{S cm}^{2}\,\text{mol}^{-1}\)

\(= (119.0 + 152.6)\,\text{S cm}^{2}\,\text{mol}^{-1} = 271.6\,\text{S cm}^{2}\,\text{mol}^{-1}\)

\(\Lambda_{m(\text{MgSO}_4)}^{\circ} = \lambda_{\text{Mg}^{2+}}^{\circ} + \lambda_{\text{SO}_4^{2-}}^{\circ} = 106.0\,\text{S cm}^{2}\,\text{mol}^{-1} + 160.0\,\text{S cm}^{2}\,\text{mol}^{-1}\)

\(= 266\,\text{S cm}^{2}\,\text{mol}^{-1}\).
_note: STALE CROSS-REFERENCE carried faithfully: the stem cites 'Table 3.4', but every table in this chapter is numbered 2.x — the limiting molar conductivities of individual ions are in Table 2.4 (printed earlier in the chapter, p-18). This is the same leftover chapter-3 numbering that appears in Eg 2.6's '(Fig. 3.7)'. No _figure attached: the book's own solution quotes every ionic conductivity it needs (119.0, 76.3, 106.0, 160.0), so the row ships answerable without the table.

stem: \(\Lambda_m^{\circ}\) for \(\text{NaCl}\), \(\text{HCl}\) and \(\text{NaAc}\) are \(126.4\), \(425.9\) and \(91.0\,\text{S cm}^{2}\,\text{mol}^{-1}\) respectively. Calculate \(\Lambda^{\circ}\) for \(\text{HAc}\).

The conductivity of \(0.001028\,\text{mol L}^{-1}\) acetic acid is \(4.95 \times 10^{-5}\,\text{S cm}^{-1}\). Calculate its dissociation constant if \(\Lambda_m^{\circ}\) for acetic acid is \(390.5\,\text{S cm}^{2}\,\text{mol}^{-1}\).
solution:
\(\Lambda_m = \dfrac{\kappa}{c} = \dfrac{4.95 \times 10^{-5}\,\text{S cm}^{-1}}{0.001028\,\text{mol L}^{-1}} \times \dfrac{1000\,\text{cm}^{3}}{\text{L}} = 48.15\,\text{S cm}^{3}\,\text{mol}^{-1}\)

\(\alpha = \dfrac{\Lambda_m}{\Lambda_m^{\circ}} = \dfrac{48.15\,\text{S cm}^{2}\,\text{mol}^{-1}}{390.5\,\text{S cm}^{2}\,\text{mol}^{-1}} = 0.1233\)

\(k = \dfrac{c\alpha^{2}}{(1-\alpha)} = \dfrac{0.001028\,\text{mol L}^{-1} \times (0.1233)^{2}}{1 - 0.1233} = 1.78 \times 10^{-5}\,\text{mol L}^{-1}\)
_note: PRINTED UNIT ERROR carried faithfully (verified at 5x zoom on p-19): the first line of the book's solution ends '\(= 48.15\,\text{S cm}^{3}\,\text{mol}^{-1}\)' — a cubic centimetre where molar conductivity requires \(\text{S cm}^{2}\,\text{mol}^{-1}\). The book refutes itself on the very next line, where the same 48.15 is written \(\text{S cm}^{2}\,\text{mol}^{-1}\) inside the \(\alpha\) ratio, and the dimensional analysis of \(\kappa/c \times 1000\,\text{cm}^{3}\,\text{L}^{-1}\) gives \(\text{S cm}^{2}\,\text{mol}^{-1}\). Only the exponent is wrong; the value 48.15 and every downstream result are correct. Left as printed for the answer-key cross-check to adjudicate rather than silently corrected. Secondary: the book writes the dissociation constant as a lower-case \(k\) in the final step, where equation (2.27) on the same page calls it \(K_a\).

stem: Why does the conductivity of a solution decrease with dilution?
Suggest a way to determine the \(\Lambda_m^{\circ}\) value of water.

The molar conductivity of \(0.025\,\text{mol L}^{-1}\) methanoic acid is \(46.1\,\text{S cm}^{2}\,\text{mol}^{-1}\). Calculate its degree of dissociation and dissociation constant. Given \(\lambda^{0}(\text{H}^{+}) = 349.6\,\text{S cm}^{2}\,\text{mol}^{-1}\) and \(\lambda^{0}(\text{HCOO}^{-}) = 54.6\,\text{S cm}^{2}\,\text{mol}^{-1}\).
A solution of \(\text{CuSO}_4\) is electrolysed for 10 minutes with a current of 1.5 amperes. What is the mass of copper deposited at the cathode?
solution:
\(t = 600\,\text{s}\); charge = current \(\times\) time \(= 1.5\,\text{A} \times 600\,\text{s} = 900\,\text{C}\)

According to the reaction:

\(\text{Cu}^{2+}(aq) + 2e^{-} = \text{Cu}(s)\)

We require \(2\text{F}\) or \(2 \times 96487\,\text{C}\) to deposit 1 mol or \(63\,\text{g}\) of Cu.

For \(900\,\text{C}\), the mass of Cu deposited \(= \dfrac{63\,\text{g mol}^{-1} \times 900\,\text{C}}{2 \times 96487\,\text{C mol}^{-1}} = 0.2938\,\text{g}\).
_note: The book writes the cathode half-reaction with an equals sign, "Cu2+(aq) + 2e- = Cu(s)", where a reaction arrow belongs. Transcribed as printed.

stem:
Write the Nernst equation and emf of the following cells at 298 K:

(i) \(\text{Mg}(s)\,|\,\text{Mg}^{2+}(0.001\,\text{M})\,||\,\text{Cu}^{2+}(0.0001\,\text{M})\,|\,\text{Cu}(s)\)

(ii) \(\text{Fe}(s)\,|\,\text{Fe}^{2+}(0.001\,\text{M})\,||\,\text{H}^{+}(1\,\text{M})\,|\,\text{H}_2(g)(1\,\text{bar})\,|\,\text{Pt}(s)\)

(iii) \(\text{Sn}(s)\,|\,\text{Sn}^{2+}(0.050\,\text{M})\,||\,\text{H}^{+}(0.020\,\text{M})\,|\,\text{H}_2(g)\ (1\,\text{bar})\,|\,\text{Pt}(s)\)

(iv) \(\text{Pt}(s)\,|\,\text{Br}^{-}(0.010\,\text{M})\,|\,\text{Br}_2(l)\,||\,\text{H}^{+}(0.030\,\text{M})\,|\,\text{H}_2(g)\ (1\,\text{bar})\,|\,\text{Pt}(s)\).

In the button cells widely used in watches and other devices the following reaction takes place:

\(\text{Zn}(s) + \text{Ag}_2\text{O}(s) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(l) \rightarrow \text{Zn}^{2+}(aq) + 2\text{Ag}(s) + 2\text{OH}^{-}(aq)\)

Determine \(\Delta_r G^{\circ}\) and \(E^{\circ}\) for the reaction.
Define conductivity and molar conductivity for the solution of an electrolyte. Discuss their variation with concentration.
The conductivity of 0.20 M solution of \(\text{KCl}\) at 298 K is \(0.0248\,\text{S cm}^{-1}\). Calculate its molar conductivity.

The resistance of a conductivity cell containing 0.001M \(\text{KCl}\) solution at 298 K is \(1500\,\Omega\). What is the cell constant if conductivity of 0.001M \(\text{KCl}\) solution at 298 K is \(0.146 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{S cm}^{-1}\).

The conductivity of sodium chloride at 298 K has been determined at different concentrations and the results are given below:

| Concentration/M | 0.001 | 0.010 | 0.020 | 0.050 | 0.100 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| \(10^{2} \times \kappa/\text{S m}^{-1}\) | 1.237 | 11.85 | 23.15 | 55.53 | 106.74 |

Calculate \(\Lambda_m\) for all concentrations and draw a plot between \(\Lambda_m\) and \(c^{1/2}\). Find the value of \(\Lambda_m^{0}\).

Conductivity of 0.00241 M acetic acid is \(7.896 \times 10^{-5}\,\text{S cm}^{-1}\). Calculate its molar conductivity. If \(\Lambda_m^{0}\) for acetic acid is \(390.5\,\text{S cm}^{2}\,\text{mol}^{-1}\), what is its dissociation constant?

How much charge is required for the following reductions:

(i) 1 mol of \(\text{Al}^{3+}\) to \(\text{Al}\)?

(ii) 1 mol of \(\text{Cu}^{2+}\) to \(\text{Cu}\)?

Three electrolytic cells A, B, C containing solutions of \(\text{ZnSO}_4\), \(\text{AgNO}_3\) and \(\text{CuSO}_4\), respectively are connected in series. A steady current of 1.5 amperes was passed through them until 1.45 g of silver deposited at the cathode of cell B. How long did the current flow? What mass of copper and zinc were deposited?

Using the standard electrode potentials given in Table 3.1, predict if the reaction between the following is feasible:

(ii) \(\text{Ag}^{+}(aq)\) and \(\text{Cu}(s)\)

(iii) \(\text{Fe}^{3+}(aq)\) and \(\text{Br}^{-}(aq)\)

(v) \(\text{Br}_2(aq)\) and \(\text{Fe}^{2+}(aq)\).
_note: STALE CROSS-REFERENCE, transcribed as printed: the book says "Table 3.1", but this chapter is Chapter 2 and its table of standard electrode potentials is Table 2.1. There is no Table 3.1 in the chapter. Almost certainly a holdover from the edition in which Electrochemistry was Chapter 3.
